caption: Your home sauna costs about 23 cents a session to run. Here's the math 👇

beats.say: A home infrared sauna costs about twenty-three cents a session.
Here's the math. A two-person infrared heater pulls about one point seven kilowatts.
Run it forty-five minutes, warm-up included, and that's about one point three kilowatt hours.
At the US average of eighteen cents a kilowatt hour, you pay about twenty-three cents.
Four sessions a week is about four dollars a month.
Comment SAUNA and I'll send you the calculator to run your own numbers.

caption: Traditional saunas cost ~$1 a session to run. Most of it is preheat.

beats.say: A traditional sauna costs about a dollar every time you use it.
The heater is usually around six kilowatts on a two-forty volt circuit.
And it runs about an hour, because forty of those minutes are just preheating the room.
Six kilowatt hours at eighteen cents is about a dollar eight.
Four times a week, that's about nineteen dollars a month.
Comment SAUNA for the free calculator.

caption: Infrared vs traditional sauna: the 30-second answer.

beats.say: Infrared or traditional sauna? Here's the thirty-second answer.
Infrared runs a hundred twenty to a hundred forty degrees. Traditional runs a hundred sixty to a hundred ninety-five.
Infrared costs about twenty-three cents a session. Traditional, about a dollar.
Want it indoors on a normal outlet? Infrared. Want real heat and steam? Traditional.
Comment SAUNA and I'll send the quiz that picks yours.

caption: Check this before you buy a sauna: your outlet.

beats.say: Before you buy a sauna, check one thing: your outlet.
Many one and two person infrared saunas plug into a normal one-twenty volt outlet.
Traditional heaters need a dedicated two-forty volt circuit.
And adding that circuit often costs three hundred to fifteen hundred dollars.
Comment SAUNA and I'll send you the cost calculator.

caption: A traditional sauna heater = four space heaters running at once.

beats.say: A traditional sauna heater is like running four space heaters at once.
A space heater uses about one point five kilowatts.
A six kilowatt sauna heater is four of those.
A small infrared sauna? Roughly one space heater.
Comment SAUNA for the free running-cost calculator.

caption: Does a $3,500 sauna beat a $50/month membership? The math.

beats.say: Does a home sauna actually beat your fifty dollar gym membership?
Say the sauna costs thirty-five hundred dollars, plus three hundred to set it up.
Power is about four dollars a month, so you save about forty-six.
That pays for itself in under seven years. Share it with a partner who'd also cancel, and it's closer to three and a third.
Comment SAUNA and run your own numbers.

caption: Live in California? Your sauna costs ~1.6x more to run.

beats.say: Where you live changes what your sauna costs to run.
The US average is about eighteen cents a kilowatt hour.
In California or New England it's closer to thirty.
So an infrared session goes from twenty-three cents to about thirty-eight.
Still cheap. Comment SAUNA for the calculator.

caption: Where your sauna's power bill actually goes: preheat.

beats.say: Most of a traditional sauna's power bill goes into an empty room.
Forty minutes of preheat for twenty minutes of sauna.
That's two thirds of the energy before you sit down.
Infrared warms you directly, so warm-up is closer to ten to twenty minutes.
Comment SAUNA and I'll send the cost calculator.

caption: What a $3,500 sauna really costs per session over 5 years.

beats.say: A thirty-five hundred dollar sauna works out to under four dollars a session.
Use it four times a week for five years. That's over a thousand sessions.
Add the price, setup and power, divide it out.
A single day pass at a spa usually costs a lot more than that.
Comment SAUNA to run your own numbers.

caption: Using a sauna 4x a week costs about $4 a month in power.

beats.say: Four sauna sessions a week costs about four dollars a month.
That's a two-person infrared at about twenty-three cents a session.
Seventeen sessions a month comes to about four dollars.
Less than one streaming subscription.
Comment SAUNA for the calculator.

caption: 3 things to check before you buy an infrared sauna.

beats.say: Three things to check before you buy an infrared sauna.
One. Does it run on a normal outlet, or need an electrician?
Two. Is the warranty five years or longer?
Three. Low-EMF heaters and real wood, like hemlock or cedar.
Comment SAUNA and I'll send the quiz that matches you to one.

caption: Where to put a home sauna (and what each spot needs).

beats.say: Where should a home sauna actually go?
A spare room or basement is perfect for infrared on a normal outlet.
Outdoors, a barrel or cabin sauna, usually traditional, on a level base.
Measure ceiling height and power before you order anything.

caption: What an outdoor barrel sauna actually costs.

beats.say: Here's what an outdoor barrel sauna actually costs.
Cedar barrel saunas from well-known makers start around fifty-four hundred dollars.
Bigger cabin models with a changing room run eight to eleven thousand.
Budget another three hundred to fifteen hundred for the electrician.
Comment SAUNA and I'll send the full cost breakdown.

caption: The cheapest way into a real infrared sauna.

beats.say: The cheapest way into a real infrared sauna is smaller than you think.
Two and three person carbon infrared saunas start around twenty-five hundred dollars.
Many plug into a regular outlet, so no electrician.
And they cost about twenty-five cents a session to run.
Comment SAUNA and I'll send the ones worth looking at.

caption: 1-person vs 2-person infrared sauna: what changes.

beats.say: One person or two person sauna? Here's what actually changes.
Both usually run around one and a half to two kilowatts.
So the running cost is almost the same, about twenty to twenty-five cents a session.
If anyone else might use it, the two-person is usually the better buy.
Comment SAUNA for the quiz.

caption: The hidden costs of a home sauna nobody mentions.

beats.say: The sticker price isn't what a home sauna costs.
Here's what gets added.
Infrared on a normal outlet skips most of it. Outdoor traditional adds the most.
Comment SAUNA and I'll send the calculator that adds it all up.

caption: Which home sauna fits you? 5 questions.

beats.say: Five questions will tell you which sauna to buy.
Indoors or outdoors. How many people. Gentle heat or real steam.
Your budget, and whether you can add a two-forty volt circuit.
That's enough to rule out most of the market.
Comment SAUNA and I'll send you the quiz.

caption: How to work out any sauna's running cost in 10 seconds.

beats.say: Here's how to work out any sauna's running cost in ten seconds.
Kilowatts, times hours, times your electricity rate.
Six kilowatts, for one hour, at eighteen cents: a dollar eight.
Find the kilowatts on the spec sheet, and your rate on your bill.
Or comment SAUNA and I'll send the calculator.

caption: Sauna + cold plunge at home: what the pair costs.

beats.say: Want a sauna and a cold plunge at home? Here's what the pair costs.
A cedar barrel sauna starts around fifty-four hundred.
A wooden cold plunge tub starts around twenty-one hundred.
So about seventy-five hundred dollars for the full backyard setup.
Comment SAUNA and I'll send the breakdown.

caption: Renting? You can still have a home sauna.

beats.say: Renting? You can still own a home sauna.
Pick a one or two person infrared that plugs into a normal outlet.
Most assemble with panels that clip together, so it moves when you move.
Check your lease and the circuit load first.

caption: Using it daily? Here's what a sauna habit costs per year.

beats.say: What does a daily sauna habit cost per year in power?
Infrared, every day: about eighty-four dollars a year.
Traditional, every day: about three hundred ninety.
Same habit, almost five times the bill.
